title: Topic 4 Tectonic hazards - Hodder practice questions

questions.question_text: Figure 4.26 shows the distribution of shallow-, intermediate- and deep-focus earthquakes. Describe the distribution of shallow-focus and deep-focus earthquakes.

points: Shallow-focus earthquakes are very widespread along almost all plate boundaries [1]
Found along divergent boundaries such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, transform boundaries like the San Andreas Fault, and destructive boundaries [1]
Deep-focus earthquakes are much less common and more restricted in distribution [1]

Deep-focus earthquakes occur almost exclusively along subduction zones at destructive plate boundaries, found inland/dip under continental plates (e.g. west coast of South America / Andes) and in island arc oceanic trenches (e.g. Kuril, Philippine, Java, Mariana Trenches) [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 4 marks. Max 2 for shallow-focus and max 2 for deep-focus descriptions with named locations.

questions.question_text: Suggest reasons to explain the distribution of shallow-focus and deep-focus earthquakes.

points: Shallow-focus earthquakes occur near the surface where brittle crust fractures under tension (divergent boundaries) or horizontal shearing (transform boundaries) [1-2]
Deep-focus earthquakes occur only where dense oceanic crust subducts beneath another plate into the hot asthenosphere/mantle [1]
As the oceanic slab plunges deeper (the Wadati-Benioff zone), friction and phase changes in minerals create deep tectonic stress up to 700 km depth [1]
Below 700 km, mantle rocks are too hot and plastic to fracture, so no earthquakes occur [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 4 marks: 2 marks for shallow-focus reasons and 2 marks for deep-focus subduction/Benioff zone reasons.

questions.question_text: Figure 4.27 shows the summit of Mount Etna in Sicily. Identify two features of the volcano shown on the photograph.

points: Craters / summit caldera / vents [1]
Steep slopes / volcanic cone / strato-volcano profile [1]
Steam / gas plume / volcanic gases emitting from vent [1]
Dark volcanic ash / tephra / lava flows / snow-covered upper flanks [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 1 mark each for two correct visual features shown in the photograph. Max 2 marks.

questions.question_text: Describe two hazards related to volcanoes.

points: Hazard 1: Pyroclastic flows — fast-moving currents of superheated gas, ash, and rock travelling down slopes at over 100 km/h, destroying everything in their path and causing asphyxiation/fatal burns [2]
Hazard 2: Lahars (volcanic mudflows) — mixture of volcanic ash and water (melted snow/heavy rainfall) rushing down river valleys at high speed, burying towns and infrastructure [2]

Alternative hazards: Ash fall (collapsing roofs, disrupting air traffic, respiratory damage), Lava flows (destroying farmland and buildings), Toxic volcanic gases (SO₂, CO₂ causing poisoning/acid rain) [2 marks each]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 2 marks for each hazard described in detail (1 mark identification, 1 mark effect/impact). Max 4 marks.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why people live in areas at risk from volcanic activity.

points: Reason 1: Fertile volcanic soils (andisols) — weathered volcanic ash and basalt are extremely rich in nutrients (potassium, phosphorus), supporting intensive farming and high crop yields (e.g. vineyards on slopes of Mt Etna, rice paddies in Indonesia) [2]
Reason 2: Geothermal energy — geothermal heat from magma reservoirs provides clean, cheap electricity and domestic heating (e.g. Iceland, New Zealand, Italy) [2]

Alternative reasons: Tourism and recreation (attracting tourists for trekking, scenery, creating jobs in hospitality); Valuable mineral extraction (sulphur, pumice, gold, copper); Family ties and poverty (inability to afford moving) [2 marks each]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 2 marks for each developed reason (1 mark point, 1 mark development). Max 4 marks.

questions.question_text: Assess the extent to which the impacts of earthquakes can be managed.

inputs.label: Nhập bài làm Case Study (7 marks):

points: Prediction: Extremely difficult; no reliable method exists to predict exact time, location, and magnitude, although seismic gap theory and animal behaviour/radon gas monitoring provide minor clues [1-2 marks]

Preparation and Protection: Highly effective in HICs through earthquake-resistant engineering (aseismic design, base isolators, counterweights, reinforced concrete, flexible gas mains), strict building codes, regular public drills (e.g. Japan Disaster Prevention Day), and early warning systems (EEW) [2-3 marks]

Contrast with LICs / Inequality: LICs lack capital to enforce building codes; shoddy construction and dense informal settlements lead to catastrophic collapse and high death tolls (e.g. Haiti 2010 vs Japan 2011) [1-2 marks]

Overall Assessment: Earthquakes cannot be prevented or predicted, but their impacts can be substantially mitigated in wealthy nations with robust preparation and building design, whereas poor nations remain acutely vulnerable [1 mark]
marking_scheme.rubric: Level 1 (1-3 marks): Simple points about managing earthquakes (e.g. building stronger houses, drills) with little detail or evaluation. Level 2 (4-6 marks): Explains specific management methods (prediction limits, aseismic building design, education, emergency response) with contrasting examples (e.g. Japan vs Haiti). Level 3 (7 marks): Comprehensive assessment evaluating both the strengths and limitations of earthquake management, explicitly linking success to level of economic development and governance, supported by specific named case studies.
